```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1236)
```


### Problem 1 — Birthday Paradox Simulation
```{r p1-01-birthday-function}
birthday_sim = function(n) {

  birthdays = sample(
    x = 1:365,
    size = n,
    replace = TRUE
  )

  shared_birthday = any(duplicated(birthdays))

  return(shared_birthday)
}
```

```{r p1-02-birthday-probability}
birthday_prob = function(n) {

  sim_results = map_lgl(
    1:10000,
    \(i) birthday_sim(n = n)
  )

  estimated_prob = mean(sim_results)

  return(estimated_prob)
}
```

```{r p1-03-all-group-sizes}
birthday_df =
  tibble(group_size = 2:50) |>
  mutate(
    probability = map_dbl(group_size, birthday_prob)
  )

birthday_df |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r p1-04-birthday-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
birthday_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of at Least Two People Sharing a Birthday",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Estimated Probability"
  )
```

The estimated probability that at least two people share a birthday generally 
increases with group size. The probability is only 0.25% for a group of two people 
but rises to 50.4% for a group of 23 people and reaches 97.1% for a group of 50 people. 
Although these results may initially seem surprising, the number of possible pairs 
increases rapidly as group size grows, making a shared birthday increasingly likely.


### Problem 2 — Longitudinal Study and Spaghetti Plot
```{r p2-01-file-names}
subject_files =
  tibble(
    files = list.files(
      "data/",
      pattern = "\\.csv$"
    ),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  )

subject_files |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r p2-02-import-data}
subject_data =
  subject_files |>
  mutate(
    data = map(path, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
  )

subject_data |>
  select(files, data)
```

```{r p2-03-unnest}
full_df =
  subject_data |>
  unnest(cols = data)

full_df |>
  select(files, week_1, week_8) |>
  head(6) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r p2-04-tidy-data}
tidy_df =
  full_df |>
  mutate(
    subj = str_remove(files, "\\.csv$"),
    arm = str_sub(subj, 1, 3),
    subject_id = str_sub(subj, 5)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week)
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, arm, subj, week, outcome) |>
  arrange(subj, week)

tidy_df |>
  head(12) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r p2-05-check-data}
nrow(tidy_df)

tidy_df |>
  count(arm) |>
  knitr::kable()

tidy_df |>
  group_by(subj) |>
  summarize(
    n_weeks = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r p2-06-spaghetti-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
tidy_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = outcome,
      group = subj,
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~ arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Outcomes by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observed Outcome",
    color = "Study Arm"
  )
```

```{r p2-07-weekly-summary}
week_summary =
  tidy_df |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarize(
    mean_outcome = mean(outcome),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

week_summary |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = arm,
    values_from = mean_outcome
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The spaghetti plot shows different longitudinal patterns between 
the control and experimental groups. Outcomes in the control group fluctuate 
over time without a clear upward or downward trend, with the group mean 
decreasing slightly from 0.915 at week 1 to 0.740 at week 8. 
In contrast, the experimental group shows a clear overall upward trend, 
with the mean outcome increasing from 1.141 to 5.119 over the same period. 
Although individual trajectories vary within both groups, 
the increase is more pronounced in the experimental group. 
These descriptive findings suggest differences in longitudinal outcome patterns 
between the two study arms, but the plot alone cannot establish a causal treatment effect.
